reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that goal-object demand varies inversely with physiological drive intensity. In the rewarded groups, the Hungry Reward group shows higher demand for the goal-object compared to the Less Hungry Reward group. This suggests a direct proportionality between drive strength and goal-seeking behavior. For non-rewarded groups, even the act of returning to the cage is more demanded under high hunger, implying that drive affects not just reward-seeking but also basic behavioral momentum. The derived ratio \( \frac{D_H}{D_{LH}} \) encapsulates this relationship mathematically. The influence of drive on behavior is modeled as \( \mathcal{F}(\text{hunger}) = \alpha \cdot \text{drive} \), which allows for quantifying how much drive modulates action selection. This framework supports both GSI’s Bayesian inference over reward likelihood and GSE’s state-transition modeling of maze navigation. Failure modes include when \( D_H \leq D_{LH} \), indicating no measurable drive effect, or when \( \text{drive} \to 0 \), leading to \( \mathcal{F} \to 0 \), suggesting no behavioral modulation.
